findings.title: Cleanup job interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
findings.body: The background cleanup ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. The clean() routine itself has a 9-minute timeout, so runs can now overlap/queue up, and all cleanup jobs (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, annotations, query history) will execute 10x more often, increasing DB load significantly. This looks like leftover debugging from reproducing the deadlock and is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR.

findings.title: Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping full ID lists
findings.body: r.log.Error(...) is used in CleanAnnotations (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 576, 579) for purely informational messages, including the entire slice of IDs being deleted. On a busy instance with large batch sizes (e.g. 32767 IDs per batch) this will spam error-level logs with huge messages every cleanup cycle, trigger alerting on error logs, and is pure debug leftover. These should be Debug level (or removed), and the ID list should not be logged.

findings.title: SQLite parameter-limit workaround keyed on batch size instead of actual ID count
findings.body: deleteByIDs decides between inlined literals and bound parameters based on r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999, not len(ids). The condition is also tied to GetDBType()==SQLite only. If any other code path (or a future caller) passes more IDs than the configured batch size, or if the configured batch size is unset/zero while a large slice is passed, the parameterized branch will be used with >999 placeholders and SQLite will fail with "too many SQL variables". Base the decision on len(ids) instead, and chunk the deletes so the statement is always within the driver limit.

findings.title: Non-atomic fetch-then-delete can loop extra times and miscount
findings.body: fetchIDs and deleteByIDs run in separate sessions, so rows found by the SELECT may already be gone when the DELETE runs. untilDoneOrCancelled only stops when affected==0, so in a concurrent scenario a batch that selects N ids but deletes 0 terminates the loop early (under-delete, as documented), but a batch that selects ids and deletes a subset keeps looping; combined with the MaxCount offset query this can repeatedly re-read the same rows. Consider terminating on len(ids)==0 rather than affected==0 so the loop semantics match the actual work remaining.
